facts: On 14 March 2026 at approximately 07:52, a Northline Logistics delivery vehicle struck the plaintiff in the marked crossing at Kellner Avenue and 7th Street.
The plaintiff sustained a comminuted fracture of the left tibia and underwent surgical fixation on 15 March 2026.
The responding officer's report records clear conditions, dry road surface, and a functioning pedestrian signal.
Northline's dispatch log shows the vehicle transmitting location data at 08:33, forty-one minutes after the driver's recorded clock-out.
The transmitted route is consistent with the assigned delivery sequence for that shift.
Northline's letter of 28 June 2026 denies liability on the basis that the driver had ended his shift.
The plaintiff's statement describes stepping into the crossing as the signal changed.
No independent witness statement has been obtained to date.

statutes.title: Comparative negligence
statutes.description: Bars recovery where the claimant's contributory fault exceeds the combined fault of all other parties; otherwise damages are reduced in proportion.
statutes.relevance: Governs the effect of any finding that the plaintiff entered the crossing early.

statutes.title: Right of way of pedestrian in crosswalk
statutes.description: Requires a driver to yield to a pedestrian lawfully within a marked crosswalk on the driver's half of the roadway.
statutes.relevance: Establishes the duty owed and supports the negligence per se argument.

statutes.title: Records of regularly conducted activity
statutes.description: Excepts from hearsay records kept in the regular course of a business activity, on foundation from a qualified witness.
statutes.relevance: The foundation route for admitting the dispatch log.

MEMORANDUM

To:       File
From:     Case Closed (AI-assisted draft)
Re:       Rivera v. Northline Logistics — vicarious liability
Date:     29 July 2026
Status:   DRAFT — FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW

QUESTION PRESENTED

Whether Northline Logistics is vicariously liable for the 14 March 2026 collision where its dispatch telemetry places the vehicle on its assigned route forty-one minutes after the operator's recorded clock-out.

BRIEF ANSWER

Probably yes, on the present record. Ohio authority treats route-completion after a recorded shift end as raising a jury question on scope of employment, and the telemetry here contradicts the employer's own timekeeping. The principal risk is comparative fault arising from the plaintiff's entry into the crossing.

ANALYSIS

An employer is answerable for the negligence of an employee acting within the scope of employment. Northline's denial rests entirely on its timekeeping record showing a 07:52 clock-out. That record is contradicted by Northline's own dispatch log, which shows the vehicle transmitting location data at 08:33 on a route consistent with the assigned delivery sequence.

Alvarado v. Crestmoor Freight Co. is directly on point: telemetry establishing that a vehicle remained on its assigned route after a recorded shift end was sufficient to reach a jury, notwithstanding the employer's timekeeping. The evidentiary posture there is the posture here.

Northline will rely on Denholm v. Riverbend Carriers, where an eleven-mile personal deviation defeated vicarious liability. Denholm is distinguishable on its facts, and its frolic-and-detour framing has since been narrowed to require a substantial rather than incidental deviation.

An independent negligent supervision count should be pleaded in the alternative under Petrakis v. Halvern Distribution, which survives even if the scope-of-employment argument does not.

OPEN ITEMS

1. Obtain municipal signal-timing records for the Kellner and 7th pedestrian phase.
2. Confirm whether Northline maintains a written policy prohibiting off-clock route completion.
3. Identify and interview any independent witness.
4. Establish the business-records foundation for the dispatch log.

seeded_chat.question: What's our exposure on comparative fault?
seeded_chat.answer:
Comparative fault is the real exposure here, and it is bounded rather than fatal.

R.C. 2315.33 reduces recovery in proportion to the claimant's share of fault and only bars it entirely if her share exceeds everyone else's combined. On these facts that threshold is unlikely to be met: the signal was functioning, conditions were clear, and R.C. 4511.46 put the duty to yield on the driver.

The closest guidance in the retrieved authority assigned twenty percent to a pedestrian who entered on a changing signal, and reduced rather than barred recovery.

The gap worth closing is the municipal signal-timing record. It would move her entry from contested to documented. I have added it to the open items in the draft.

Three soft spots, in order of how much they matter.

First, there is no independent witness. The plaintiff's own statement describes stepping in as the signal changed, and nothing corroborates the sequence from outside the parties.

Second, comparative fault. The entry-on-a-changing-signal fact pattern has drawn a twenty percent apportionment in the closest retrieved authority — recovery reduced, not barred, but it prices the claim.

Third, foundation for the dispatch log. The whole scope-of-employment theory runs through that record, so it must come in as a business record under Evid.R. 803(6); line up the custodian early.

None of these is disqualifying, and each has a concrete fix in the open items.
